quote: Maybe that which you would do even if there were no morality, is your morality.
content: Offered as a comforting line of retreat, this is a substantive and implausible metaethical thesis: it identifies what is right for you with what you would in fact do absent any normative constraint. The book elsewhere denies it emphatically. "Ends Don't Justify Means" holds that what you would do when your calculations tell you to seize power is precisely what your morality must forbid, and "Ethical Injunctions" is built on the premise that your dispositions in the moment are the untrustworthy part. What you would do without morality includes akrasia, cowardice, cruelty under provocation, and every failure the reader recognizes in themselves; a theory that ratifies all of it as their morality has given up the distinction between what one does and what one should do, which is the distinction the concept exists to mark.

quote: Otherwise you would be committing what is known (appropriately) as The Genetic Fallacy: causation is not the same concept as justification.
content: The genetic fallacy shield is applied selectively. Evolutionary debunking arguments — Street's "A Darwinian Dilemma for Realist Theories of Value" (Philosophical Studies 127, 2006) is the canonical statement — do not infer falsity from origin; they argue that a belief-forming process selected for fitness rather than truth gives us no reason to expect its outputs to track independent moral facts, which is an evidential argument about reliability, not a genetic fallacy. That is exactly the argument this book runs against religious belief, at length, in Books I and II: your faith was produced by a process that would have produced it whether or not it were true. A metaethics that accepts the argument in one place and calls it a fallacy in the other needs to say what distinguishes the cases. The essay's own answer, given three essays later, is that morality is not supposed to track anything external — which concedes the debunker's premise rather than refuting it.

quote: Only evolutionary biologists even know how to define genetic fitness, and they know better than to think it defines morality.
content: Both halves are shakier than they sound. Evolutionary ethics is a live tradition rather than a confusion outsiders fall into: Spencer built a system on it, E. O. Wilson's Sociobiology closed by proposing that ethics be "biologicized," and Ruse and Wilson's "Moral Philosophy as Applied Science" (Philosophy 61, 1986) argued the case in a philosophy journal — the position is wrong, in my view, but it is held by people who do know how fitness is defined. And the definition itself has been contested within biology, most publicly in the dispute over inclusive fitness set off by Nowak, Tarnita, and Wilson's 2010 Nature paper and the response signed by well over a hundred biologists. "The experts have this settled and agree with me" is an appeal that this book teaches readers to check.

quote: There’s a difference between a calculator that calculates
content: The calculator analogy answers the wrong worry. It shows that a computation performed in your head need not be a computation about your head, which disposes of the crude subjectivism that whatever you think is right is thereby right. It does nothing about the objection that actually threatens the position, which is the one the Pebblesorters raise: two calculators may implement different functions, each returning what is correct by its own lights, with no further fact settling which function is the right one to run. The 2 + 3 example works because arithmetic supplies an external standard that both calculators are answerable to. Supplying the analogue of that standard for morality is the whole problem, and the analogy assumes it.
